cases.title: Pitch matching in choir singers and instrumentalists
cases.context: In a study looking at pitch matching (singing back a tone that was just heard), adult amateur musicians were asked to sing back a 220 hertz (Hz) target tone. A response was scored as accurate when the sung pitch was within 50 cents (half of a semitone) of the target. The table below shows the number of accurate singers among choir singers (group 1) and among instrumentalists who do not sing regularly (group 2).
tasks: (i) Calculate the proportion of accurate singers in each group and the difference, choir singers minus instrumentalists.
(ii) What is the 95% margin of error for this difference? What is the 95% confidence interval for the difference in the proportion of accurate singers between the two groups?

(iii) Using only your calculations for Parts (i) and (ii), is the difference in the proportion of accurate singers between these two groups statistically significant with \(P<0.05\)? Please state how you reached your conclusions.

hypotheses.nullWords: The proportion of accurate singers is the same for choir singers and instrumentalists.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The proportion of accurate singers is different for choir singers and instrumentalists.

cases.symbols: \(m_i\) (accurate singers), \(n_i\) (musicians tested), \(\hat p_i\) (sample proportion), \(\hat p\) (pooled proportion), \(s_{\hat p_1-\hat p_2}\) (SE of the difference), \(z_{0.05}\) (two-sided Normal cutoff), \(M\) (margin of error).

steps.title: Find both sample proportions
steps.words: The procedure is a 95% confidence interval for the difference between two proportions, built from the margin of error. Each proportion is the number of accurate singers divided by the number of musicians tested in that group.

steps.title: Find the observed difference
steps.words: Keep the direction choir singers minus instrumentalists throughout.

steps.title: Pool the two groups
steps.words: Both groups are pooled to estimate one common proportion for the standard error.

steps.title: Calculate the standard error of the difference
steps.words: Multiply the pooled variance term by the sum of the reciprocal group sizes, then take the root.

steps.title: Read the Normal cutoff
steps.words: Open t_table.pdf, PDF page 2, and use the infinity row in the 0.05 two-tail column. The infinity row is the standard Normal cutoff, 1.960.

steps.title: Calculate the margin of error
steps.words: This product is the number that a report prints after "plus or minus".

steps.title: Form the interval and decide
steps.words: Zero lies outside the interval because the observed difference is larger than its margin of error, so the null hypothesis of equal proportions is rejected at the two-sided 0.05 level.

cases.conclusion: The choir minus instrumentalist difference is 14.7 percentage points plus or minus 10.76 points (95% CI 0.0391 to 0.2543). The interval does not contain 0, so there is a difference in the proportion of accurate singers between the two groups, with the higher proportion among choir singers (P < 0.05).

cases.title: Mind wandering with the phone on the desk
cases.context: Researchers interested in mind wandering (attention drifting away from the task to unrelated thoughts) did a study with a 40 minute recorded statistics talk. Students were randomly assigned to watch with their phone face down on the desk (group 1) or with the phone left in another room (group 2). At a single thought probe (a prompt that stops the talk and asks what the student was just thinking about), each student reported being on task or mind wandering. The table below shows the results.
tasks: (i) Calculate the proportion of students who reported mind wandering in each group and the difference, phone on desk minus phone in another room.
(ii) What is the 95% margin of error for this difference? What is the 95% confidence interval for the difference in the proportion of students who reported mind wandering between the two groups?

(iii) Using only your calculations for Parts (i) and (ii), is the difference in the proportion of students who reported mind wandering between these two groups statistically significant with \(P<0.05\)? Provide your result in a single complete sentence that would convey your conclusion in a way that could be understood by a non-expert in statistics or medicine (e.g., a typical reader of a local newspaper).

hypotheses.nullWords: The proportion of students who report mind wandering is the same with the phone on the desk and with the phone in another room.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The proportion of students who report mind wandering is different with the phone on the desk and with the phone in another room.

cases.symbols: \(m_i\) (students who reported mind wandering), \(n_i\) (students), \(\hat p_i\) (sample proportion), \(\hat p\) (pooled proportion), \(s_{\hat p_1-\hat p_2}\) (SE of the difference), \(z_{0.05}\) (two-sided Normal cutoff), \(M\) (margin of error).

steps.title: Find both sample proportions
steps.words: The procedure is a 95% confidence interval for the difference between two proportions, built from the margin of error. Each proportion is the number of students who reported mind wandering divided by the number of students in that group.

steps.title: Find the observed difference
steps.words: Keep the direction phone on desk minus phone in another room throughout.

steps.title: Pool the two groups
steps.words: Both groups are pooled to estimate one common proportion for the standard error.

steps.title: Calculate the standard error of the difference
steps.words: Multiply the pooled variance term by the sum of the reciprocal group sizes, then take the root.

steps.title: Read the Normal cutoff
steps.words: Open t_table.pdf, PDF page 2, and use the infinity row in the 0.05 two-tail column. The infinity row is the standard Normal cutoff, 1.960.

steps.title: Calculate the margin of error
steps.words: This product is the number that a report prints after "plus or minus".

steps.title: Form the interval and decide
steps.words: Zero lies inside the interval because the observed difference is smaller than its margin of error, so the null hypothesis of equal proportions is not rejected at the two-sided 0.05 level.

cases.conclusion: The phone on desk minus phone in another room difference is 5.1 percentage points plus or minus 11.53 points (95% CI -0.0640 to 0.1666). The interval contains 0, so there is no evidence of a difference (P > 0.05). In plain words, this study does not show that keeping the phone on the desk changes how often students' minds wander.

cases.title: Earplugs and noise notches in orchestra musicians
cases.context: A study was reported concerning hearing in 400 professional orchestra musicians. Each musician was classified by whether earplugs were usually worn in rehearsal, and pure-tone audiometry (measuring the quietest tone a person can hear at each frequency) was done. A noise notch was recorded when the hearing threshold at 4 kilohertz (kHz) was at least 15 decibels hearing level (dB HL) worse than the threshold at 2 kHz. The musicians had chosen for themselves whether to wear earplugs. The table below shows the results.
tasks: (i) Use a chi-square test. Is there a difference in the proportion of musicians with a noise notch between the two groups?
(ii) Calculate the relative risk of a noise notch for the earplug group relative to the group without earplugs.
(iii) Can it be concluded from this study that wearing earplugs caused the difference? Please state how you reached your conclusions.

hypotheses.nullWords: The proportion of musicians with a noise notch is the same in the earplug group and in the group without earplugs.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The proportion of musicians with a noise notch is different in the earplug group and in the group without earplugs.

cases.symbols: \(n_{TD}\) (musicians with a notch in the earplug group), \(n_T\) (earplug group size), \(n_{CD}\) (musicians with a notch in the group without earplugs), \(n_C\) (size of the group without earplugs), \(O\) (observed count), \(E\) (expected count), \(RR\) (relative risk).

steps.title: Find the group totals
steps.words: The procedure is a chi-square test for a 2×2 table, followed by a relative risk. Add the musicians with and without a notch in each row. The grand total is 400 and 84 musicians have a notch.

steps.title: Calculate expected counts
steps.words: Expected counts are what each cell would hold if the proportion with a notch were the same in both groups.

steps.title: Calculate the Yates-corrected chi-square
steps.words: Subtract one half from each absolute difference between observed and expected before squaring. This is the Yates correction, used for every 2×2 table.

steps.title: Compare with the chi-square cutoff
steps.words: Open Chi_Squared_Table1.pdf, page 1, row 1. Start with α = 0.05, where the cutoff is 3.841. The statistic exceeds it, so the null hypothesis is rejected. It also exceeds the 0.025 cutoff of 5.024 but not the 0.01 cutoff of 6.635, so 0.01 < P < 0.025.

steps.title: Calculate both proportions
steps.words: Each proportion is the risk of a noise notch within that group.

steps.title: Calculate the relative risk
steps.words: The risk of a noise notch in the earplug group is about 57% of the risk in the group without earplugs.

steps.title: State what the design allows
steps.words: The musicians chose whether to wear earplugs and were not assigned at random. The two groups may also differ in instrument, seat position or years of playing, so the result is an association and does not show that earplugs caused the lower risk.

cases.conclusion: The null hypothesis is rejected (chi-square = 6.405, 1 df, 0.01 < P < 0.025). There is a difference in the proportion of musicians with a noise notch between the two groups. The relative risk is 0.5656, so the risk in the earplug group is about 57% of the risk without earplugs. Because the musicians chose their own group, this is an association and not proof that earplugs caused the difference.

cases.title: Balance training and falls in older adults
cases.context: In a clinical trial, 298 adults aged 70 years or older were randomly assigned to 6 months of balance training (standing and stepping exercises on an unstable surface) or to a stretching program. Each person then kept a fall diary for 12 months, and a person was counted as a faller after at least one fall. The table below shows the results.
tasks: (i) Use a chi-square test. Is there a difference in the proportion of fallers between the two groups?
(ii) Calculate the relative risk of falling for the balance training group relative to the stretching group.
(iii) What does the way the groups were formed allow the researchers to conclude? Please state how you reached your conclusions.

hypotheses.nullWords: The proportion of fallers is the same in the balance training group and in the stretching group.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The proportion of fallers is different in the balance training group and in the stretching group.

cases.symbols: \(n_{TD}\) (fallers in the balance training group), \(n_T\) (balance training group size), \(n_{CD}\) (fallers in the stretching group), \(n_C\) (stretching group size), \(O\) (observed count), \(E\) (expected count), \(RR\) (relative risk).

steps.title: Find the group totals
steps.words: The procedure is a chi-square test for a 2×2 table, followed by a relative risk. Add the fallers and the people with no fall in each row. The grand total is 298 and 75 people fell at least once.

steps.title: Calculate expected counts
steps.words: Expected counts are what each cell would hold if the proportion of fallers were the same in both groups.

steps.title: Calculate the Yates-corrected chi-square
steps.words: Subtract one half from each absolute difference between observed and expected before squaring. This is the Yates correction, used for every 2×2 table.

steps.title: Compare with the chi-square cutoff
steps.words: Open Chi_Squared_Table1.pdf, page 1, row 1. Start with α = 0.05, where the cutoff is 3.841. The statistic is smaller than the cutoff, so the null hypothesis is not rejected and P > 0.05. It does exceed the 0.10 cutoff of 2.706, so 0.05 < P < 0.10.

steps.title: Calculate both proportions
steps.words: Each proportion is the risk of at least one fall within that group.

steps.title: Calculate the relative risk
steps.words: In this sample the risk of falling in the balance training group is about 70% of the risk in the stretching group.

steps.title: State what the design allows
steps.words: The groups were formed by random assignment, so a significant difference could have been credited to the training. Here the difference is not significant, so a sample relative risk below 1 is not evidence that the training lowers the risk. A relative risk of 1 remains compatible with these data.

cases.conclusion: The null hypothesis is not rejected (chi-square = 2.785, 1 df, 0.05 < P < 0.10). There is no evidence of a difference in the proportion of fallers between the two groups. The sample relative risk is 0.6952, but with these group sizes a value this far from 1 can arise by chance. The random assignment would allow a causal conclusion, but only if the difference were significant.

cases.title: Speech in noise and age in musicians and non-musicians
cases.context: Researchers interested in how hearing speech in noise changes with age did a study with 22 musicians and 23 non-musicians aged 20 to 75 years. For each person the speech reception threshold (SRT, the signal-to-noise ratio at which half of the sentences are repeated correctly, so a lower value is better) was measured in decibels (dB). Separate R regressions of SRT (dB) on Age (years) were run for the two groups with lm(SRT ~ Age). The Age rows of the two R coefficient tables and the residual standard errors are shown below.
tasks: (i) State the null hypothesis and the alternative hypothesis for the two slopes in symbols and in words.
(ii) Calculate the standard error of the difference between the two slopes and the t statistic. Make sure to show your intermediate calculations.
(iii) Based on your calculations, is the trend between SRT and Age different in the two groups? Give the degrees of freedom, the critical value from the printed t table and the P range.

hypotheses.nullWords: The mean SRT of musicians and non-musicians rises with age at the same rate.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The rate at which the mean SRT rises with age is different for musicians and non-musicians.

cases.symbols: \(b_M, b_N\) (sample slopes for musicians and non-musicians), \(s_{b_M}, s_{b_N}\) (slope standard errors), \(s_{b_M-b_N}\) (SE of the slope difference), \(\nu\) (degrees of freedom).

steps.title: Read both slopes and standard errors
steps.words: The procedure is a t test that compares two regression slopes. Take the Age row of each R coefficient table, where the Estimate column is the slope and the Std. Error column is its standard error.

steps.title: Calculate the slope difference
steps.words: The difference is negative. In these samples the SRT of musicians worsens by about 0.056 dB less per year of age than the SRT of non-musicians.

steps.title: Calculate the SE of the difference
steps.words: The two samples are independent, so the variances of the two slopes add.

steps.title: Calculate the t statistic
steps.words: Divide the slope difference by its standard error.

steps.title: Find df and the critical value
steps.words: Four degrees of freedom are lost because each line estimates an intercept and a slope. Open t_table.pdf, PDF page 1. The table has no row for 41, so use the next lower printed row, 40, which gives the slightly larger and therefore conservative cutoff of 2.021 in the two-tail 0.05 column.

steps.title: Decide and bracket P
steps.words: Start with α = 0.05. The magnitude of the statistic exceeds 2.021, so the null hypothesis of equal slopes is rejected. It also exceeds the 0.02 cutoff of 2.423 but not the 0.01 cutoff of 2.704, so 0.01 < P < 0.02.

cases.conclusion: The null hypothesis of equal slopes is rejected (t = -2.456, 41 df read from row 40, 0.01 < P < 0.02). There is a difference in the trend between SRT and Age in the two groups. The mean SRT worsens more slowly with age in musicians (0.0316 dB per year) than in non-musicians (0.0879 dB per year).

cases.title: Pitch discrimination on practice and training, least squares by matrix
cases.context: The table below shows data on 16 adult violinists. For each violinist the pitch discrimination threshold (the smallest pitch difference between two tones that can be heard reliably) was measured in cents, where 100 cents is one semitone, so a lower threshold means a finer ear. The threshold is y, weekly practice in hours (h) is x1 and formal training in years is x2. A multiple regression of y on x1 and x2 is to be fitted by the matrix least-squares formula, with the matrix inverse taken from software.
tasks: (i) Build \(X^TX\) and \(X^Ty\) from the sums of the data.
(ii) Solve \(b=(X^TX)^{-1}X^Ty\) for \(b_0, b_1, b_2\) and write the fitted equation.
(iii) Use \(SS_{res}\) to find \(s_{y|x}\) and \(R^2\). Make sure to show your intermediate calculations.
cases.symbols: \(X\) (design matrix with a column of ones, then x1 and x2), \(y\) (threshold vector), \(b\) (coefficient vector), \(SS_{res}\) (sum of squared residuals), \(SS_{tot}\) (total sum of squares), \(k\) (number of independent variables), \(s_{y|x}\) (residual standard error).

steps.title: Build the cross-product matrix
general: X^TX=\begin{bmatrix}n&\sum x_1&\sum x_2\\\sum x_1&\sum x_1^2&\sum x_1x_2\\\sum x_2&\sum x_1x_2&\sum x_2^2\end{bmatrix}
steps.words: The procedure is a multiple regression fitted by least squares. Each entry is a sum over the 16 violinists. The first row and column come from the column of ones.

steps.title: Build the cross-product vector
steps.words: Multiply each column of X by the threshold values and add.

steps.title: Invert the cross-product matrix
steps.words: The inverse is found with software. Its diagonal entries are used again later for the coefficient standard errors.

steps.title: Solve for the coefficients
steps.words: Multiply the inverse by the cross-product vector. R prints the same values, 50.8416, -0.8097 and -1.2825, in the Estimate column of summary(lm(y ~ x1 + x2)). Both slopes are negative, so more practice and more training go with a lower threshold.

steps.title: Calculate the residual variance
steps.words: Three parameters are estimated, so 13 degrees of freedom remain. The root is the Residual standard error that R prints as 3.497.

steps.title: Calculate R squared
steps.words: About 81% of the variation in the threshold is accounted for by weekly practice and years of training together. R prints Multiple R-squared 0.8131.

cases.conclusion: The least-squares plane is ŷ = 50.84 − 0.8097x1 − 1.2825x2 (cents), with s_y|x = 3.497 cents on 13 df and R² = 0.8131. Each extra hour of weekly practice goes with a threshold about 0.81 cents lower at a fixed number of training years.

cases.title: Vigilance lapses on sleep and ADHD symptom score
cases.context: Researchers interested in sustained attention did a study with 24 university students. Each student did a 10 minute psychomotor vigilance task (PVT, pressing a button as soon as a counter appears on a screen), and the number of lapses (responses slower than 500 milliseconds (ms)) was counted. Number of lapses ("Lapses"; lapses in the 10 minute task) is the dependent variable; sleep the night before ("Sleep"; hours) and score on an adult attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder symptom scale ("ADHD"; 0 to 54, where a higher score means more symptoms) are the independent variables. The R call summary(lm(Lapses ~ Sleep + ADHD)) printed the output below.
tasks: (i) Based on the R results, show how you would reject the null hypothesis of no relation between the number of lapses and all of the variables above (i.e., the null hypothesis that all of the coefficients are zero). Provide the alternate hypothesis as part of your answer. Recompute F from the printed R-squared and give the critical value from the printed F table.
(ii) Based on the R results, which explanatory variables are statistically significant? What is the 95% confidence interval for each of the two slopes?
(iii) Estimate the number of lapses of a student that slept 6 hours and has an ADHD score of 30. You can do this calculation by-hand.

hypotheses.nullWords: Neither the hours of sleep nor the ADHD symptom score is related to the mean number of lapses.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: At least one of the two variables, hours of sleep or ADHD symptom score, is related to the mean number of lapses.

cases.symbols: \(R^2\) (multiple R-squared), \(k\) (number of independent variables), \(n\) (number of students), \(MS_{mod}, MS_{res}\) (model and residual mean squares), \(b_j\) (coefficient), \(s_{b_j}\) (its standard error).

steps.title: Find the F degrees of freedom
steps.words: The procedure is the F test for a multiple regression as a whole. Two independent variables are tested together, and 21 degrees of freedom remain for the residuals.

steps.title: Recompute F from R squared
steps.words: Dividing SS_mod and SS_res by SS_tot turns them into R² and 1 − R², so F can be checked from the printed R². R prints 26.31 because it uses unrounded values.

steps.title: Compare with the F cutoff
steps.words: Open F_table.pdf, page 1, numerator column 2, denominator row 21. Start with α = 0.05, where the lightface value is 3.47. The boldface value for 0.01 is 5.78. F exceeds both, so the null hypothesis is rejected with P < 0.01 from the table. R gives P = 1.907e-06.

steps.title: Test the Sleep coefficient
steps.words: Open t_table.pdf, PDF page 1, row 21, where the 0.05 column gives 2.080. The magnitude also lies between 3.527 (0.002) and 3.819 (0.001), so 0.001 < P < 0.002, which agrees with the 0.00114 that R prints. Sleep is statistically significant.

steps.title: Test the ADHD coefficient
steps.words: The ADHD coefficient is also statistically significant, and the statistic exceeds the 0.001 cutoff of 3.819, so P < 0.001. R prints 5.315 because it divides the unrounded estimate by the unrounded standard error.

steps.title: Build 95% intervals for both slopes
steps.words: Neither interval contains 0, which agrees with both t tests.

steps.title: Predict by hand
steps.words: Substitute 6 hours of sleep and an ADHD score of 30 into the fitted equation. The result is a mean number of lapses.

cases.conclusion: The null hypothesis of no relation is rejected (F = 26.31 on 2 and 21 df, P < 0.01 from the printed table and P = 1.907e-06 from R). Both explanatory variables are statistically significant. More sleep goes with fewer lapses (t = -3.765, 0.001 < P < 0.002) and a higher ADHD score goes with more lapses (t = 5.312, P < 0.001). The predicted mean for 6 hours of sleep and an ADHD score of 30 is about 11.5 lapses.

cases.title: Toddler vocabulary with summary, confint, refit and prediction
cases.context: Researchers interested in early language did a study with 30 toddlers aged 18 to 30 months. Expressive vocabulary (the number of different words the child says, taken from a parent checklist) is the dependent variable; age ("Age"; months), adult words heard per day ("AdultWords"; thousands of words, counted by a small recorder worn by the child) and screen time ("Screen"; hours per day) are the independent variables. R printed the summary() output, the confint() output, and a second summary() after the analysis was re-done with only the explanatory variables that were statistically significant.
tasks: (i) Write the full regression equation. Based on the R results, show how you would reject the null hypothesis of no relation between vocabulary and all of the variables above (i.e., the null hypothesis that all of the coefficients are zero).

(ii) Based on the R results, which explanatory variables are statistically significant? Based on the confint() confidence intervals, make an inference about the significance of each explanatory variable. Do these results agree with your conclusions from the t tests?

(iii) Using the resulting regression equation (the analysis re-done with only the explanatory variables that were statistically significant), estimate the vocabulary of a 24-month-old child that hears 15 thousand adult words per day. DO NOT use R.

hypotheses.nullWords: Screen time has no relation to mean vocabulary once age and adult words are in the model.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: Screen time is related to mean vocabulary once age and adult words are in the model.

cases.symbols: \(b_j\) (coefficient estimate), \(s_{b_j}\) (standard error), \(k\) (number of independent variables), \(\nu=n-k-1\) (residual degrees of freedom), \(\hat y\) (predicted mean vocabulary).

steps.title: Write the full equation
steps.words: The procedure is a multiple regression read from R output. Read the Estimate column of the full summary.

steps.title: Test the model as a whole
steps.words: The null hypothesis is that none of the three variables is related to mean vocabulary. Open F_table.pdf, page 1, numerator column 3, denominator row 26. Start with α = 0.05, where the lightface value is 2.98. The boldface value for 0.01 is 4.64. F exceeds both, so the null hypothesis of no relation is rejected with P < 0.01. R gives P = 2.432e-09.

steps.title: Test each coefficient
steps.words: Compare each magnitude with the 0.05 cutoff of 2.056 in t_table.pdf, PDF page 1, row 26. Age and AdultWords exceed it, so they are statistically significant. Screen does not (R prints P = 0.321), so Screen is not statistically significant.

steps.title: Confirm with the 95% intervals
steps.words: The Screen interval worked by hand matches confint() to rounding. It contains 0, while the Age and AdultWords intervals do not contain 0, which agrees with the t tests.

steps.title: Refit without Screen
steps.words: The refit coefficients change slightly because Screen no longer shares the explanation. Both remaining t values (9.677 and 4.126 on 27 df) exceed 3.690, the 0.001 cutoff in row 27, so P < 0.001 for each.

steps.title: Predict by hand
steps.words: Substitute an age of 24 months and 15 thousand adult words per day into the refit equation.

cases.conclusion: The model as a whole is significant (F = 35.48 on 3 and 26 df, P < 0.01). Age and AdultWords are statistically significant, but Screen is not (t = -1.011, and its interval contains 0). The refit gives ŷ = -320.6071 + 18.4472·Age + 5.7755·AdultWords, and the predicted mean vocabulary of a 24-month-old who hears 15 thousand adult words per day is about 208.8 words.

cases.title: Probability and odds of detecting a tone in noise
cases.context: In a study looking at the detection of a quiet tone in background noise, one listener did 40 trials. On each trial a 1 kilohertz (kHz) tone was presented at a level between 0 and 18 decibels sound pressure level (dB SPL), and the listener answered yes (heard, coded 1) or no (not heard, coded 0). R fitted glm(Detect ~ Level, family = "binomial") by maximum likelihood and printed the coefficient table below.
tasks: (i) Based on the R output, is the trend between the probability of detecting the tone and Level statistically significant?
(ii) What is the probability of detecting a tone of 12 dB SPL?
(iii) The odds of detecting the tone for a 12 dB SPL tone are __ : 1.

hypotheses.nullWords: The probability of detecting the tone does not change with the level of the tone.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The probability of detecting the tone changes with the level of the tone.

cases.symbols: \(b_0, b_1\) (maximum-likelihood estimates), \(x\) (tone level in dB SPL), \(p\) (probability of detecting the tone), \(z\) (estimate divided by its standard error).

steps.title: Test the Level coefficient
steps.words: The procedure is logistic regression, because the outcome is yes or no. Use the infinity row of t_table.pdf, PDF page 2, for the Normal cutoffs, which are 1.960 at 0.05 and 3.2905 at 0.001. The statistic exceeds both, so the null hypothesis is rejected with P < 0.001. R prints 0.000913.

steps.title: Form the linear predictor
steps.words: The linear predictor is the logit, the natural log of the odds.

steps.title: Convert to a probability
steps.words: The logistic function keeps the result between 0 and 1. Rounded to two places, p = 0.61.

steps.title: Calculate the odds
steps.words: Dividing the rounded probability 0.61 by 0.39 gives 1.56. Carrying p unrounded gives 1.57, and rounding p to two places causes the small difference.

cases.conclusion: The trend between the probability of detecting the tone and Level is statistically significant (z = 3.316, P < 0.001). A 12 dB SPL tone has an estimated detection probability of 0.6110 (0.61), so the odds of detecting it are about 1.56 to 1 from the rounded probability (1.57 to 1 unrounded).

cases.title: Absolute pitch and the age at which lessons began
cases.context: A study was reported concerning absolute pitch (naming a musical note with no reference tone) in 50 conservatory students. Each student took a note-naming test and was scored as having absolute pitch (coded 1) or not (coded 0). The age at which music lessons began (StartAge, in years) was recorded and ranged from 3 to 14 years. R fitted glm(AP ~ StartAge, family = "binomial") and printed the coefficient table below.
tasks: (i) Based on the R output, is the trend between the probability of absolute pitch and StartAge statistically significant?
(ii) What is the probability of absolute pitch for a student who began lessons at age 4? What is it for a student who began at age 12?
(iii) The odds of absolute pitch for a student who began lessons at age 4 are __ : 1.
(iv) By what factor do the odds of absolute pitch change for each additional year of StartAge?

hypotheses.nullWords: The probability of absolute pitch does not change with the age at which lessons began.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The probability of absolute pitch changes with the age at which lessons began.

cases.symbols: \(b_0, b_1\) (maximum-likelihood estimates), \(x\) (age at which lessons began, in years), \(p\) (probability of absolute pitch), \(e^{b_1}\) (odds multiplier per year).

steps.title: Test the StartAge coefficient
steps.words: The procedure is logistic regression, because the outcome is yes or no. Use the infinity row of t_table.pdf, PDF page 2, for the Normal cutoffs. The magnitude exceeds the 0.05 cutoff of 1.960 and the 0.02 cutoff of 2.3263, but it falls just short of the 0.01 cutoff of 2.5758. The null hypothesis is rejected with 0.01 < P < 0.02. R prints 0.0103.

steps.title: Probability for lessons from age 4
steps.words: For a student who began at age 4 the estimated probability of absolute pitch is about 0.59.

steps.title: Probability for lessons from age 12
steps.words: The slope is negative, so the probability falls as the starting age rises. For a student who began at age 12 it is about 0.15.

steps.title: Odds for lessons from age 4
steps.words: Both routes give the same odds, about 1.46 to 1. Odds above 1 mean that absolute pitch is more likely than not at this starting age.

steps.title: Odds multiplier per year
steps.words: Each additional year before lessons begin multiplies the odds of absolute pitch by about 0.767, a 23% decrease in the odds.

cases.conclusion: The trend between the probability of absolute pitch and StartAge is statistically significant (z = -2.566, 0.01 < P < 0.02). The estimated probability is 0.5937 for lessons from age 4 and 0.1495 for lessons from age 12. The odds of absolute pitch at a starting age of 4 are about 1.46 to 1, and the odds fall by a factor of 0.7674 for each additional year.

questions.stem: In the pitch matching study, 67 of 150 choir singers and 48 of 160 instrumentalists sang within 50 cents of the target. What is the 95% margin of error for the difference between the two proportions?
questions.why: The margin of error is the Normal cutoff 1.960 times the pooled standard error 0.05490. The other values are the standard error alone, the standard error times 1.645, and the difference itself.

questions.stem: A report on a thought-probe study states that the proportion of students who were mind wandering was 5.1 percentage points higher with the phone on the desk, plus or minus 11.5 points (95% margin of error). What does this result show?
options: There is no evidence of a difference, because the 95% interval for the difference contains 0.
There is a difference, because the observed difference is above 0.
There is a difference, because the margin of error is larger than the difference.
The two proportions are proven to be equal, because the margin of error is larger than the difference.
questions.why: The interval runs from about −6.4 to 16.6 points and contains 0, so equal proportions are not rejected at the 0.05 level. Not rejecting is not proof that the proportions are equal.

questions.stem: A noise notch was found in 23 of 160 orchestra musicians who usually wore earplugs and in 61 of 240 who did not. What is the relative risk of a noise notch, earplug group relative to the group without earplugs?
questions.why: The relative risk divides the earplug-group proportion 0.14375 by the proportion without earplugs 0.25417. Inverting the ratio, using the raw counts, or using the odds gives the other values.

questions.stem: Two studies report a relative risk of falling below 1 for older adults who do balance training. In study A the adults chose for themselves whether to train. In study B the adults were randomly assigned to training or to stretching. If both results are statistically significant, which study supports the claim that the training itself lowered the risk?
options: Study A, because people who choose to train are more motivated.
Study B, because random assignment makes the groups alike in everything except the training.
Both equally, because the relative risk is below 1 in both.
Neither, because a relative risk can never show cause.
questions.why: With self-chosen groups, fitter or more careful people may be the ones who train, so the result is only an association. Random assignment balances such differences, so a significant result can be credited to the training.

questions.stem: R gives a slope of SRT on Age of 0.0316 dB per year (SE 0.0134) for 22 musicians and 0.0879 dB per year (SE 0.0186) for 23 non-musicians. What is the t statistic for the null hypothesis that the two slopes are equal?
questions.why: The slope difference −0.0563 is divided by the root of the sum of the squared standard errors, 0.02292. Adding the standard errors without squaring, or testing one slope against zero, gives the other values.

questions.stem: For 16 violinists the fitted plane is ŷ = 50.84 − 0.81x1 − 1.28x2, where ŷ is the pitch discrimination threshold (cents), x1 is weekly practice (hours) and x2 is years of training. What does the coefficient −0.81 say?
options: A violinist who practices one more hour per week has a threshold exactly 0.81 cents lower.
Practice explains 81% of the variation in the threshold.
At a fixed number of training years, each extra hour of weekly practice goes with a mean threshold about 0.81 cents lower.
Each extra hour of weekly practice goes with a mean threshold about 0.81 cents lower, whatever happens to the years of training.
questions.why: A multiple regression coefficient is the change in the mean of y for a one-unit change in that variable while the other variables are held fixed. It describes the mean, not each person, and it is not a proportion of variation.

questions.stem: For lm(Lapses ~ Sleep + ADHD) with 24 students, R prints Multiple R-squared 0.7147. What F statistic for the model as a whole follows from this R-squared?
questions.why: F divides R²/k by (1 − R²)/(n − k − 1) with k = 2 and n − k − 1 = 21. Leaving out both degrees of freedom, leaving out k, or using n − 1 = 23 gives the other values.

questions.stem: The refit of toddler vocabulary on the significant variables is ŷ = -320.6071 + 18.4472·Age + 5.7755·AdultWords. What is the predicted mean vocabulary of a 24-month-old child who hears 15 thousand adult words per day?
questions.why: Substitute Age = 24 and AdultWords = 15 into the refit equation. Swapping the two values, using the full-model coefficients without Screen, or dropping the intercept gives the other values.

questions.stem: R fits glm(Detect ~ Level, family = "binomial") and gives an intercept of -5.19637 and a Level coefficient of 0.47065. What is the estimated probability of detecting a 12 dB SPL tone?
questions.why: The linear predictor is −5.19637 + 0.47065(12) = 0.45143, and the logistic function turns it into p = 0.6110. The value 0.4514 is the logit, 1.5706 is the odds, and 0.3890 is the probability of not detecting the tone.

questions.stem: A logistic regression of absolute pitch (yes or no) on the age at which music lessons began gives a StartAge coefficient of −0.26473 with P = 0.0103. What does the negative coefficient say?
options: The probability of absolute pitch falls by 0.26473 for each additional year.
Starting age is not related to absolute pitch, because the coefficient is below 0.
The odds of absolute pitch are multiplied by about 0.767 for each additional year, so the probability falls as the starting age rises.
The odds of absolute pitch are 0.26473 to 1 at every starting age.
questions.why: The coefficient is the change in the log odds per year, so the odds are multiplied by e to the power −0.26473, which is 0.767. A multiplier below 1 means the probability falls as x rises.

notes: All data are invented for practice. The raw data behind every R table are stored in check_session19b.py (DATA), and the script refits each lm() and glm() model with statsmodels and compares every printed number.

R output is carried the same way as in the reference cases (a table of coefficient rows plus one summary row). P values are written with 3 significant digits, which is close to but not always identical to the digit count R would choose.

As in the reference cases, `values` for the R-output cases are computed from the printed (rounded) R numbers, because that is what a student works from. This is why the hand F (26.30) and the hand t for ADHD (5.312) differ in the last digit from the R output (26.31 and 5.315). The step words say so.

n19-b-speech-noise-slopes has 41 df, which is not a printed row of the t table. The solution uses row 40 (2.021, 2.423, 2.704) as the conservative row and sets lookup.approximation to true with actualDf 41. The P range 0.01 < P < 0.02 is the same with the exact 41 df.

n19-b-speech-noise-slopes keeps the reference key names in `values` (bM, sbM, bF, sbF, nM, nF). Here M is musicians and the F keys hold the non-musician group, written with the subscript N in the LaTeX.

The two multiple regression test cases name their t and interval keys after their own variables (tSleep, tADHD, ciSleep, ciADHD, tScreen, ciScreen, refitAdultWords, adultWords), in the same pattern as tMother, ciBMI and refitExercise in the reference cases. The logistic cases do the same (level, p4, p12, oddsPerYear, halfwayAge), and n19-b-absolute-pitch-start-age adds one key, odds4, for the odds task.
The key oddsSlide is kept from the reference logistic case. It holds the odds worked from the probability rounded to two places.
Step-level table lookups use the key classTable, as the reference cases do.

Outcomes are mixed. n19-b-mind-wandering-margin and n19-b-balance-training-falls do not reject, Screen is not significant in the vocabulary case, and the absolute pitch slope lands just short of the 0.01 Normal cutoff (|z| = 2.566 against 2.5758).
The odds tasks keep the requested wording "are __ : 1", which is the only colon left in a task. The solutions write the odds as "1.56 to 1".
n19-b-balance-training-falls quotes the 0.10 chi-square cutoff 2.706 (Chi_Squared_Table1.pdf, row 1) to bracket P between 0.05 and 0.10.

Style review: the two R-summary cases now state the variables in the homework's own form ("Name"; unit) is the dependent variable; ... are the independent variables, and their tasks carry his wording (i.e., the null hypothesis that all of the coefficients are zero). These are the only semicolons in context and tasks, and check_session19b.py allows colons and semicolons there.
